heard: The moon's brightest rocks are too young to exist. Apollo missions found bright rocks called anorthosite that form the lunar highlands. Experts thought these rocks floated to the surface of a global magma ocean. This coarse-grained rock is 90% plagioclase feldspar, which is less dense than liquid magma. But in 2011, researchers dated lunar sample 60,025 to only 4.36 billion years old. This age is far too young for a crust formed during the moon's birth. Now scientists think the crust formed slowly through many volcanic eruptions. New theories are rewriting lunar history to explain why the moon's brightest rocks are too young to exist.
